items.stem: What is a user-defined data type?
options: A variable entered by the user
A data type built into the language such as INTEGER
A data type designed by the programmer, built from existing data types
A type of file
items.answer: A data type designed by the programmer, built from existing data types
items.markingKey: e.g. enumerated, pointer, record, set, class.

items.stem: Explain why a programmer might use an enumerated data type instead of an integer code.
items.answer: Values have meaningful names, making code easier to read and maintain; only the listed values are allowed, which reduces errors; values are ordered so can be compared.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a non-composite and a composite data type.
items.answer: A non-composite type is defined without reference to other data types (e.g. enumerated, pointer); a composite type is built from other data types (e.g. record, set, class).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Atlas Museum stores 100 customer records in a random file with 200 locations. The key is a 6-digit customer number. (a) Write a pseudocode function Hash(Key : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER using the MOD operator. (b) Write pseudocode that uses Hash to find the record for a key input by the user, using the next free location for collisions; use SEEK and GETRECORD. (c) Explain why the file has more locations than records.
items.answer:
FUNCTION Hash(Key : INTEGER) RETURNS INTEGER
    RETURN Key MOD 200
ENDFUNCTION

INPUT SearchKey
Address ← Hash(SearchKey)
OPENFILE "Customers.dat" FOR RANDOM
Found ← FALSE
Count ← 0
WHILE NOT Found AND Count < 200
    SEEK "Customers.dat", Address
    GETRECORD "Customers.dat", Customer
    IF Customer.Key = SearchKey THEN
        Found ← TRUE
    ELSE
        Address ← (Address + 1) MOD 200
        Count ← Count + 1
    ENDIF
ENDWHILE
CLOSEFILE "Customers.dat"
(c) Spare locations reduce the number of collisions and the length of probe sequences.
items.markingKey: (a) header and RETURN Key MOD n [2] (b) open RANDOM [1]; SEEK and GETRECORD [1]; compare key [1]; move to next location with wrap [1]; loop termination [1] (c) [1]

items.stem: Records are stored in a random file with 7 locations (0 to 6) using address = key MOD 7. A collision is resolved by storing the record in the next free location (wrapping to 0). The keys 751, 979, 805, 182, 758 are inserted in order. Give the address where each key is stored.
items.markingKey: 751 MOD 7 = 2; 979 MOD 7 = 6; 805 MOD 7 = 0; 182 MOD 7 = 0, collision, stored at 1; 758 MOD 7 = 2, collision, stored at 3. Award 3 for all correct, deduct 1 per error [3]

items.stem: A random file uses address = key MOD 7 with collisions placed in the next free location. Its contents are: [0] empty, [1] 218, [2] 225, [3] 535, [4] 232, [5] 955, [6] empty. Describe how the record with key 232 is found and state the number of locations read.
items.answer: Hash 232 MOD 7 = 1; read location 1, not the key, so read the following locations until it is found at 4. 4 reads.

items.stem: Sofia is the systems analyst for Nova Telecom. Discuss whether Nova Telecom should use sequential or direct (random) access for its customer file.
items.answer: Points in favour: direct access finds individual records quickly for online enquiries; sequential access is efficient for batch processing of every record (e.g. monthly bills). Points against / limitations: random files need a hashing algorithm and collision handling, and waste space; sequential files are slow for single-record look-ups. Conclusion: direct access suits interactive use; sequential suits batch runs; an indexed sequential file can give both.
items.markingKey: Up to 3 marks for relevant technical points correctly applied to the scenario; up to 3 marks for developed explanation that weighs both sides and reaches a justified conclusion. Indicative content: direct access finds individual records quickly for online enquiries; sequential access is efficient for batch processing of every record (e.g. monthly bills). / random files need a hashing algorithm and collision handling, and waste space; sequential files are slow for single-record look-ups. [6]

items.stem: Sofia is designing a hashed file for Horizon Travel with 11 locations (0 to 10); the hash is Key MOD 11 and a collision uses the next free location. (a) Insert the keys 837, 372, 906, 928, 119 in this order and give the location of each key. (b) Explain what is meant by a collision and how linear probing deals with it.
items.answer: (a) 837 → 1; 372 → 9; 906 → 4; 928 → 5; 119 → 10 (b) Two keys hash to the same address; the record is placed in the next free location (wrapping round).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per correct location, max 4 [4] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why a programmer might use an enumerated data type instead of an integer code. (b) Explain the difference between a non-composite and a composite data type.
items.answer: (a) Values have meaningful names, making code easier to read and maintain; only the listed values are allowed, which reduces errors; values are ordered so can be compared. (b) A non-composite type is defined without reference to other data types (e.g. enumerated, pointer); a composite type is built from other data types (e.g. record, set, class).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point, max 2 [2] (b) 1 mark each [2]

items.stem:
Study the pseudocode.
TYPE TIntPointer = ^INTEGER
DECLARE Level, Other : INTEGER
DECLARE MyPointer : TIntPointer
Level ← 34
MyPointer ← @Level
Other ← 9
MyPointer ← @Other
MyPointer^ ← MyPointer^ + Level
OUTPUT Level, " ", Other
State the output.
items.markingKey: MyPointer is moved to point at Other, so only Other changes: 9 + 34 = 43 [2]

items.stem: Ravi is writing a program for GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Doha that manages staff rotas. (a) Explain how a class differs from a record. (b) Describe a situation in which a set type would be useful.
items.answer: (a) A class contains methods (procedures/functions) as well as attributes, and supports encapsulation; a record has data fields only. (b) e.g. storing the days on which a member is available and testing membership or finding common days with intersection.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark situation; 1 mark operation [2]
